sentences.text: The genus name Cryptoclidus translates to "hidden clavicles," referring to the animal's small, nearly invisible collar bones that were buried within its shoulder girdle.
The specific epithet "eurymerus" means "wide femur," a label applied because the forelimb was originally mistaken for a hindlimb.
The largest known individuals of this species measured up to 4 meters in length and weighed between 737 and 756 kilograms.
The genus Cryptoclidus was formally described by Seeley in 1892.
The type species was initially described under the name Plesiosaurus eurymerus before being reclassified.
Fossils have been recovered from the Oxford Clay of Cambridgeshire, England.
A dubious species, Cryptoclidus beaugrandi, is known from Kimmeridgian-age deposits in Boulogne-sur-Mer, France.
The species Cryptoclidus vignalensis, now considered undiagnostic, originates from the Jagua Formation of western Cuba.
A 2016 report described a fragmentary skeleton from Russia, though later research defined it as an intermediate cryptoclidid.
To adapt to marine life, Cryptoclidus transformed its limbs into long, narrow flippers.
Recent discoveries indicate that the bone structure of its trunk allowed the animal to live only in the water.
Cryptoclidus belongs to the family Cryptoclididae.
It is classified within the subfamily Cryptoclidinae.
Cryptoclidus lived during the Middle Jurassic to Late Jurassic periods, specifically from the Callovian to the Oxfordian stages.
The time range for this genus is estimated to be from 165.3 to 143.1 million years ago.
Fossils have been found in England, France, and Cuba.
It is debated whether a specific Russian fossil fragment belongs to Cryptoclidus or represents an intermediate form between Cryptoclidus and other cryptoclidids.
